answer: Hypothesis (data-grounded): Summed social capital (Copper&Gold + Amber + Monument Count) peaked in the 14th century BCE (BCE 1400, tied with BCE 1300 at z-sum = +4.24, Older Bronze Age period group) — a plateau spanning the 14th–13th centuries BCE, with the adjacent centuries 1200/1100 BCE close behind (+3.62). The rise into this peak was driven primarily by Copper & Gold (+2.90 z into the peak — the largest single-century rise anywhere in the series; +3.14, 46% of the total long-run increase) and secondarily by Monument Count (+1.54 into the peak; +2.63, 38.5% overall), while Amber contributed the least to the Bronze Age peak (+0.60 into the peak; 15.5% overall). Amber instead drove an earlier, separate social-capital hump in the Neolithic (+2.53 jump at 4000 BCE; its sign-flipped PCA loading confirms it moves on a different axis). A sign-fixed PCA (PC1, 48.6% of variance; loadings CopperGold +0.68, MonumentCount +0.66, Amber −0.31) supports a "Bronze Age metal-plus-monument" axis of rising social capital. The peak is robust: 3-century centered rolling mean → BCE 1300; linearly detrended sum → BCE 1400; interpolated annual sum → BCE 1400 (flat plateau 1400–1300 BCE); century-aggregated annual mean → BCE 1400. Pollen/openness context: openness (Belau+Woserin PC1 mean) correlates weakly and negatively with summed social capital over the 3,399-year overlap (Spearman −0.21 annual; −0.23 century-level) and reaches its maximum only later (~800 BCE), so the capital peak is not explained by, and precedes, maximal landscape openness.

payload.peak_century: BCE 1400 (tied with BCE 1300; sum z = +4.24, OBA)

drivers.CopperGold: +3.14 over run-up (46.0%), +2.90 jump into peak (largest single-century rise in series)
drivers.Amber: +1.06 (15.5%), +0.60 into peak; instead drives earlier Neolithic hump (BCE 4000, +2.53)

payload.hypothesis: Summed social capital peaked in the 14th-13th century BCE plateau (BCE 1400/1300, Older Bronze Age, z-sum +4.24), driven mainly by Copper & Gold and Monument Count; Amber contributed least to that peak and instead underpinned an earlier Neolithic capital hump; landscape openness (pollen PC1) correlates weakly negatively and peaks only ~800 BCE, so the social-capital peak precedes maximal openness.
